bridge: Use invented notes for this exercise. You need a file manager, a browser and a plain-text editor, such as Notepad or TextEdit in plain-text mode.
teaching:
### Find where a file lives

A file stores information, such as a note or picture. A folder groups files. A path is the address of a file within those folders. If two folders each contain notes.txt, the names match but the paths identify different files.

Create a folder called cyber-notes in a place you can find again. Inside it, create a folder called copies. This gives your practice work an obvious home.

### If this is your first saved text file

The file manager is the app used to browse folders: Finder on macOS or File Explorer on Windows. Make cyber-notes in your Documents folder, then make copies inside it. Wait until each new folder has its intended name before opening it.

Use a plain-text editor such as Notepad on Windows. In TextEdit on macOS, choose Format, then Make Plain Text before saving. A word processor may otherwise save formatting rather than the .txt file we need. Use Save As to choose cyber-notes and the name week1.txt. If the editor adds .txt for you, do not add it twice.

To make the backup, select week1.txt in the file manager, choose Copy, open copies and choose Paste. Rename the pasted file week1-backup.txt. Do not choose an alias or shortcut: those point to the same file instead of making an independent copy.

To record a location, use the file manager's location display or file information. Write the folders from Documents down to the filename. On Windows this might begin C:\Users\your-name\Documents; on macOS it might begin /Users/your-name/Documents. Your actual account name and location will differ. The extension is the ending .txt, not the whole filename.

### Save and reopen one note

Open a plain-text editor, type the supplied lines and save them as week1.txt inside cyber-notes. Plain text stores the characters without a word processor's page formatting. Check the full filename; some systems hide familiar extensions such as .txt.

Close the editor, find the file in the file manager and reopen it. This checks that you saved to the location you intended rather than merely leaving text in an open window.

### Distinguish your copy from the original

Copy week1.txt into copies and rename the copy week1-backup.txt. For now, both files should contain the same three lines. In the practice task, you will add a line only to the original and check that the backup stays unchanged. An ordinary copy is independent; it is not automatically a live synchronised document.

Downloading a handout also gives you a copy. Renaming that copy does not rename the teacher's online original. Keep the page URL when you need to return to the source.

### Read a web address

In https://example.org/course/start, https is the scheme: it names how the browser should connect. example.org is the host: the website name. /course/start is the path: the requested location within that website. The / in a URL is not a folder instruction to type into your text editor. Keep the complete URL when recording where a downloaded file came from.
example:
cyber-notes/
  week1.txt
  copies/
    week1-backup.txt

week1.txt contents:
Question: Where is my work saved?
Action: Created a local text file.
Result: Reopened it after closing the editor.
explanation: Use your system's file manager to create cyber-notes and its copies subfolder. Open a plain-text editor, type the three log lines and save as week1.txt inside cyber-notes. Close the editor, locate the file in the file manager and reopen it. Copy it into copies as week1-backup.txt. Reopen both: at this point their three lines should match. Leave the original unchanged until the practice task tells you to add a fourth line. That later comparison will demonstrate that the copy is independent.
exercise:
1. If you followed the worked example, use those saved files. Otherwise create the shown folders and the three-line week1.txt, then copy it to copies/week1-backup.txt.
2. Open only week1.txt. Add a fourth line: Next: learn account safety. Save and close it.
3. Reopen the original and backup from the file manager. Do not rely on text left in an unsaved editor window.
4. Write the full location of each file, its extension, and the text that appears only in the original. No terminal is required.
solution:
Your locations should end in cyber-notes/week1.txt and cyber-notes/copies/week1-backup.txt. On Windows the folder separator may appear as a backslash. The part before cyber-notes depends on where you saved your folder.

Both files have the .txt extension. Both contain the three supplied lines beginning Question, Action and Result. Only the original has the fourth line, “Next: learn account safety.” The original therefore has four lines and the backup three.

If both changed, check that you opened two different paths and made a copy rather than a shortcut. If you cannot find either file after closing the editor, return to Save As and check the chosen location.
challenge: Without the walkthrough, create a separate practice2 folder with an original note and a recovery copy. Close every editor, find both files and demonstrate which is the newer copy. Explain the scheme, host and path of https://example.org/course/start.
challenge_solution: An independent copy survives closing the editor. For the URL: scheme https, host example.org, path /course/start. A convincing submission gives file locations and observed contents; a screenshot of an open unsaved editor is insufficient.
example_intro: Read this as a folder diagram, not as commands. A name ending in / is a folder. Indented names sit inside the folder above them. Create the folders with your file manager; type only the three labelled content lines into the note.
